INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
American Atheists, Inc., is a national 501(c)(3) civil
rights organization that works to achieve religious
equality for all Americans by protecting what Thomas
Jefferson called the “wall of separation” between government and religion created by the First Amendment.
American Atheists strives to promote understanding
of atheists through education, advocacy, and communitybuilding; works to end the stigma associated with
atheism; and fosters an environment where bigotry
against our community is rejected. As a membership
organization representing the interests of atheists
and nonreligious people across the country, American
Atheists opposes any effort to create or expand
religious exemptions to generally applicable laws or to
grant religious claimants privileged access to the
judicial system.
INTRODUCTION
This case is not about a man merely seeking to host
a prayer or a study group around his dinner table. Far
from simply hosting occasional religious get-togethers,
Mr. Grand took steps to convert a room in his home to
a house of worship, inviting dozens of people to gather
multiple times every week on the sabbath. He did this
despite his home being in an area zoned for residential
use, where his neighbors rely on the other properties
in the neighborhood being used for residential
purposes, where the city planners have established

1 Amicus has no parent company nor have they issued stock.
No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part, and
no party or counsel for a party made a monetary contribution
intended to fund its preparation or submission. No person other
than amicus made a monetary contribution to the preparation or
submission of this brief.

2
infrastructure and utilities designed to support typical
residential use, where traffic controls are carefully
calibrated for residential street and pedestrian traffic,
and where property values are calculated with the
natural assumption that other properties in the area
will be used in accordance with zoning laws. For
property owners seeking to use their property in ways
that do not conform to those zoning laws, the city has
created procedures and processes to request special
use permits or changes to the zoning laws themselves.
Nevertheless, Mr. Grand insists that he is entitled to
ignore zoning regulations because his reasons are
religious. He refuses to follow the procedures and rules
that apply to everyone else because he has religious
motivations. He not only demands that the city allow
him to proceed with his nonconforming use of his
property while he seeks a permit for that use, but also
that he is entitled to skip those procedures entirely
because his nonconforming use is religious in nature.
This case is an attempt to push us further along the
path Congress first started down with the passage of
the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Every step
takes “us further down a perilous path in forcing
States to entangle themselves with religion, with all of
our rights hanging in the balance.” Kennedy v.
Bremerton Sch. Dist. , 597 U.S. 507, 578 (2022),
Sotomayor, J., dissenting. Every step down this path
exacerbates an injustice: religious Americans have
more rights than anyone else.  If you are religious, you
get special causes of action. 42 U.S.C. § 2000bb-1(c); 42
U.S.C. § 2000cc-2(a). If you are religious, you can
exempt your child from any school assignment that
runs afoul of your beliefs (especially if the lesson
acknowledges the existence of the LGBTQ community).
You can count your donations to opaque, unaccountable,

3
and largely unregulated religious entities as tax
deductible. You can create “religious” for-profit corporations and ignore regulations you dislike (especially
if your aim is to deny your employees access to
reproductive health care). You can take taxpayer
money and disregard nondiscrimination laws. You can
deny your children access to medical care (especially if
you deny them vaccines). And if this Court agrees with
Mr. Grand, if you are religious, you will be allowed to
ignore zoning procedures.
This abuse of the First Amendment must end. The
Establishment Clause “means at least this: Neither a
state nor the Federal Government can . . . pass laws
which aid one religion, aid all religions, or prefer one
religion over another.” Everson v. Bd. of Educ. of Twp.
of Ewing , 330 U.S. 1, 15 (1947). With this case, the
Court is “yet again paying almost exclusive attention
to the Free Exercise Clause’s protection for individual
religious exercise while givi ng short shrift to the
Establishment Clause’s prohibition on state establishment of religion.” Kennedy, 597 U.S. at 546 (Sotomayor,
J., dissenting).
Mr. Grand doesn’t want the inconvenience of having
to continue walking to the synagogue he previously
attended. Grand v. City of Univ. Heights, 159 F.4th 507,
509 (2025). One sympathizes. But that minor inconvenience does not entitle him to an exemption from
basic zoning regulations nor from procedural requirements this Court has established for land-use litigation.
“To make an individual’s obligation to obey such a law
contingent upon the law’s coincidence with his
religious beliefs, except where the State’s interest is
‘compelling’ -- permitting him, by virtue of his beliefs,
‘to become a law unto himself,’ -- contradicts both
constitutional tradition and common sense.” Employment

4
Div. v. Smith , 494 U.S. 872, 885 (1990) (quoting
Reynolds v. United States, 98 U.S. 145, 167 (1878)).
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
By his own words, Mr. Grand  sought to establish a
house of worship in his home in a neighborhood not
zoned for that use. He described his intended use as a
shul and a beis hakeneset, both terms being synonyms
for a synagogue. He invited a dozen families to attend
and bring their friends. And he stated his intention to
grow his new congregation.
Mr. Grand did all this without completing the
process of applying for a special use permit. Those
zoning laws exist to ensure that University Heights,
like many municipalities, can adequately plan infrastructure projects and provide sufficient services to its
residents. Zoning laws impact traffic flows, public
safety, and the provisions of water, sewer, and waste
management services to neighborhoods. Mr. Grand
ignored all of that and did not bother to go through the
process of obtaining a final decision on his application
for a special use permit, preferring to go straight to
court with an unripe claim and an incomplete factual
record. He demands the right to do this because his
intended nonconforming use was religious in nature.
Creating an exception to the established ripeness
doctrine for land-use cases would impair the ability of
the judiciary to review land-use decisions by necessarily limiting the information available to the courts.
It would create significant risk of harm to municipalities and their residents. Finally, it would set a
dangerous precedent, paving the way for religious
litigants seeking redress for any number of claims to
come straight to court while the rest of us deal with

5
Article III’s standing, ripeness, and justiciability
requirements.
For these reasons, the Court should affirm the
decision below.
ARGUMENT
Mr. Grand claims that this case is about a “prayer
meeting” but it is about far more than that. John
Fritze, The little-noticed Supreme Court case that
could impact where people pray , CNN (Aug. 11, 2026,
10:12 AM), https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/10/politics/
prayer-supreme-court-religious-zoning. He asserts that
special justiciability rules should apply to religious
claimants. The ramifications of that assertion, should
this Court side with him, could reach into virtually
every aspect of the law. Ultimately, he is asking this
Court to issue a rule that would effectively exempt
houses of worship and other religious uses of land from
any zoning regulations.
I. Grand expressly intended to establish a
house of worship.
Contrary to much of the public discourse surrounding this case, see id., Mr. Grand was not seeking to host
an informal prayer group in his home. Nor do the
actions of University Heights threaten the ability of
anyone to have such get-togethers in their own homes.
Rather, in the email he sent out announcing his
endeavor, he made it very clear that he was creating a
house of worship.
Religion is not a wand one can wave to absolve
oneself of any and all legal obligations. Mr. Grand did
not seek to merely hold a “prayer meeting” in his home.
Id. He specifically invited roughly a dozen households,
whom he encouraged to “spread the word to whomever

6
you feel might be interested in coming,” to attend
“the inauguration of the Shomayah Tefillah Beis
Hakeneset,” Grand v. City of Univ. Heights , No. 1:22-
cv-1594, 2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 176340, at *4 (N.D.
Ohio Sept. 30, 2024), for multiple meetings every
sabbath, id. Mr. Grand stated specifically, “I know that
the intended recipient of my email understood what I
meant because they are my friends and they knew that
I was converting my residential home into a formal
synagogue that would be re ady to be inaugurated a
few days later.” J.A. 187. He recruited a rabbi. Grand,
2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS at *4. He referred to it as a
“shul” intended to “expand the community” by reaching
a new neighborhood and provide a “place where people
come to seriously daven,... a powerful place to have
your prayers heard and answered.” Id. at 4-5.
The parties may quibble over the fuzzy outer
boundaries of the term “house of worship” as used in
University Heights’ zoning regulations but that
discussion is not relevant here. Mr. Grand was quite
clear in his intention. His email announced the
formation of a new synagogue. “Beis hakeneset” (or its
alternative spellings, “beit knesset” and “beit k’neset”)
literally translates to “house of gathering” or “house of
assembly” and denotes a synagogue. Beit Knesset ,
Jewish English Lexicon (accessed October 26, 2026),
https://jel.jewish-languages.org/words/51; Beit k’neset,
ReformJudaism.org (accessed October 26, 2026), https://
reformjudaism.org/glossary/beit-kneset; Synagogue: Beit
Haknesset, Chabad.org (accessed October 6, 2026),
https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/580840
5/jewish/Synagogue-Beit-Haknesset.htm. The term shul
denotes a synagogue as well. Shul, Jewish English
Lexicon (accessed October 26, 2026), https://jel.jewishlanguages.org/words/543; Shul, ReformJudaism.org
(accessed October 26, 2026), https://reformjudaism.

7
org/glossary/shul; The Synagogue (Shul), Chabad.org
(accessed October 26, 2026), https://www.chabad.org/li
brary/article_cdo/aid/365929/jewish/The-Synagogue.htm.
A synagogue is unequivocally a house of worship.
University Heights officials were justifiably concerned
that Mr. Grand intended to  use his property in a
manner that did not conform to the local zoning
regulations and, as a result, could put a significant
strain on the infrastructure in his neighborhood. His
attempt to use his home as a shul or beis hakeneset
was not University Heights’ first experience with a
resident establishing their home as a “residential
shul.” Around the same time Mr. Grand sent his
inaugural email to roughly a dozen families, University
Heights had been forced to take another resident to
court for operating one in an area not zoned for it.
Grand, 2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS at *7 n.2. That
congregation was hosting roughly 120-130 individuals
in the basement of a house. Id. Any building regularly
hosting such a substantial number of people could put
a significant strain on city infrastructure that roads
and sidewalks, as well as water, power, and solid waste
management systems, in an area zoned for purely
residential use were never intended to support.
Although Mr. Grand sent his initial email to
approximately 12 area households, he also encouraged
them to bring anyone else who was interested and
expressly stated that he intended to recruit additional
attendees from nearby neighborhoods. Id. at 4-5. That
he started by emailing a dozen families does not mean
that only 12 individuals would attend. To the contrary,
he seemed intent on growing his new congregation
significantly. Id. City officials were rightly concerned.

8
II. Creating a religious exception to Williamson
County’s final decision rule creates a twotiered classification for property owners
and would set a dangerous precedent.
This Court, in Williamson County Regional Planning
Commission v. Hamilton Bank , determined that a
plaintiff bringing a constitutional challenge against a
land-use regulation must at least receive a final
decision from the regulating governmental body in
order for a claim to be ripe for judicial review. 473 U.S.
172, 187 (1985). Williamson County ’s final-decision
requirement is not an arbitrary imposition of red tape.
This Court offered several significant justifications
for the requirement, all of which hold regardless of
whether the land owner’s motivations are sectarian or
secular.
First, Williamson County’s requirement addresses a
fundamental issue of justiciability: a concrete injury.
Absent a final decision, it is “not clear whether the
[government] would deny approval” of the use in
question. Id. at 187. Furthermore, requiring a claimant
to receive a final decision from the applicable
governing body before resorting to litigation provides
an opportunity for the parties involved to reach “a
mutually acceptable solution…, thereby obviating any
need to address the constitutional questions.” Id.
Second, the final-decision requirement protects the
rights of others with an interest in how the land is
used. It affords an opportunity  for other parties to be
heard through applicable notice-and-comment requirements. Id. at 189. It also allow s for the consideration
of “the economic impact of the challenged action and
the extent to which it interferes with reasonable
investment-backed expectations,” factors “of particular
significance in the [land-use] inquiry.” Id. at 191.

9
“Those factors simply cannot be evaluated until the
administrative agency has arrived at a final, definitive
position regarding how it will apply the regulations at
issue to the particular land in question.”
Disregarding these important considerations simply
because the land owner is motivated by religious
considerations would set a precedent with far-reaching
ramifications, both in the context of land use and in
numerous other areas of law.
A. Ripeness requirements are necessary
for the functioning of the judiciary.
Article III of the U.S. Constitution has no carve-out
for questions involving religion. The mere fact that one
seeking approval of a development plan, a variance or,
in this instance, a “special use permit” is doing so
for religious reasons does not make any of the
considerations laid out in Williamson County  less
relevant to the question of ripeness.
Justiciability criteria like ripeness do not exist
simply to provide judges with an opportunity to
engage in thought exercises. These criteria exist to
ensure the courts stay within the bounds imposed by
Article III. U.S. Const. art. III, § 2. The “basic rationale”
of ripeness doctrine:
is to prevent the courts, through avoidance of
premature adjudication , from entangling
themselves in abstract disagreements over
administrative policies, and also to protect
the agencies from judicial interference until
an administrative decision has been formalized and its effects felt in a concrete way by
the challenging parties.
Abbott Lab’ys v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136, 148-49 (1967)
(emphasis added), superseded by statute on other

10
grounds, 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1). Until “the initial
decisionmaker has arrived at a definitive position on
the issue,” the factual record is incomplete and it is
mere speculation whether the government’s decision
would “inflict[] an actual, concrete injury.” Williamson
Cnty. Reg’l Plan. Comm’n, 473 U.S. at 193-94.
The possibility of reaching a “mutually acceptable
solution” can still obviate any need to resort to litigation to address a constitutional question. Id. at 187.
Likewise, the fact that the owner’s intended use is
religious does not change the fact that, until a final
decision is reached, the possibility remains that the
land owner will be able to use their property exactly as
they intend without need for judicial intervention. Id.
Finally, the fact that an intended use is religiously
motivated does not change the myriad ways granting
a variance might impact neighbors and the municipality itself.
Mr. Grand sought to host worship services multiple
times each sabbath. Because he abandoned his
attempt to obtain a special use permit, the record is
incomplete. The Court does not know how many people
Mr. Grand intended to host. It does not know if he
intended there to be a cap on the number of attendees.
It does not know how a congregation of the size Mr.
Grand intended would have impacted pedestrian
traffic every Friday and Saturday or increased the
needs of his neighborhood for water, waste management, and other utilities. In short, because Mr. Grand
did not bother to obtain a final decision on his
application for a special use permit, the Court only has
one side of the equation: it knows the burden placed on
Mr. Grand’s religious exercise but cannot know the
burden that an accommodation would impose on
University Heights and its residents. It must perform

11
a balancing test where one side of the scale holds
nothing but question marks.
B. Eliminating the Williamson County
finality requirement for religious litigants will harm municipalities and
their residents.
This Court has long recognized the important
function that zoning laws and regulations serve:
There is no serious difference of opinion in
respect of the validity of laws and regulations
fixing the height of buildings within reasonable limits, the character of materials and
methods of construction, and the adjoining
area which must be left open, in order to
minimize the danger of fire or collapse, the
evils of over-crowding, and the like, and
excluding from resident ial sections offensive
trades, industries and structures likely to
create nuisances.
Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., 272 U.S. 365 (1926).
University Heights estab lished its zoning plan to
address the public concerns acknowledged by the
Court. The city adopted its plan “for the protection and
promotion of the public health, safety, convenience,
comfort, prosperity and the general welfare.” University
Heights, Ohio, Zoning Code § 1242.01(a). The city
aimed to guide future development within its boundaries:
…for the most beneficial land use and population density; . . . to reduce or avoid the need for
general traffic flow on local residential streets,
especially truck traffic ; to insure adequate
open space between buildings, especially for
residential occupancy; to provide a guide for

12
public policy and action in the economical
provision of public facilities and services and
for related public needs , and a guide for
private enterprise in building development,
investment and other economic activity
relating to the uses of land and buildings.
University Heights, Ohio, Zoning Code § 1242.01(b)
(emphasis added).
Public safety is a serious concern to all municipalities and zoning regulations play a significant role in
preserving that safety. An obvious concern that arises
when a building plays host to 100 people when it
was designed to play host to a fraction of that is the
risk of fire. Overcrowded buildings create a heightened
risk of fires and the Ohio fire code and local fire
departments place occupancy limits on buildings
specifically to minimize that risk and exceeding those
limits can create an actionable nuisance. City of
Cincinnati v. Risconi Bar & Kitchen, LLC, 1st Dist.
Hamilton, No. C-260057, 2026-Ohio-4130, ¶ 4.
Moreover, the procedure for obtaining a special
use permit from the University Heights Planning
Commission provides an opportunity for neighbors to
be heard, requiring at least seven days’ notice to be
“given to the record owners of parcels within 100 feet
from the exterior boundaries of the area described in
the application, and to the record owners of other
parcels deemed by the Commission to be immediately
affected by the case, and to members of Council.”
University Heights, Ohio, Zoning Code § 1220.09.
Regardless of whether his reasons are religious,
Grand’s neighbors deserve an opportunity to be heard
if he is going to host 20 or 50 or 120 people in his house
multiple times per week. The issuance of a special use
permit could impose burdens on neighbors that weigh

13
heavily against granting an accommodation. Estate of
Thornton v. Caldor, Inc., 472 U.S. 703, 708-10 (1985).
This Court has been particularly creative of late
when interpreting the Establishment Clause but it
still “means at least this: Neither a state nor the
Federal Government can . . . pass laws which aid one
religion, aid all religions, or prefer one religion over
another.” Everson v. Bd. of Educ. of Twp. of Ewing, 330
U.S. 1, 15 (1947).  Without the complete record that
would accompany a final decision, Mr. Grand’s
neighbors would be denied any opportunity to be heard
in a matter that may directl y affect their day-to-day
lives and property interests purely because Mr.
Grand's reasons were religiou s. With this case, the
Court is poised to “yet again pay[] almost exclusive
attention to the Free Exercise Clause’s protection for
individual religious exercise while giving short shrift
to the Establishment Clause’s prohibition on state
establishment of religion.” Kennedy , 597 U.S. at 546
(Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
Because Mr. Grand sought to skip the line and come
straight to court before obtaining a final decision on
his application for a special use permit, it is impossible
to say whether University Heights would have considered any or all of these factors when assessing his
application for a special use permit. Would the flow of
pedestrian traffic have presented a risk of significant
increases in vehicle-pedestrian collisions on Friday
nights and Saturdays? Would increased waste disposal
demands have required more frequent visits from
sanitation trucks, or required the roads to accommodate larger sanitation trucks? Would the neighborhood’s
sewer system be overburdened on Fridays and
Saturdays as a result of Mr. Grand’s nonconforming
use? Each of these questions have answers. The courts

14
need those answers to decide land-use cases. Yet none
of those answers can be found in the record because
Mr. Grand demands privileged access to the courts
before his claim was ripe for judicial review. That
his motivation was religious does not change this
simple fact of how our judicial system functions under
Article III.
C. Exempting religious claimants from
Williamson County’s prudential requirements sets a dangerous precedent that
would have ramifications in numerous
other contexts.
We have been here before  and we have seen where
this leads. This Court issues a sound, reasonable
decision that brings together a line of cases and
discerns from those cases a rule that is both sound and
reasonable. See generally Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S.
602 (1971). However, when t hat rule results in a
decision that a majority of justices on this Court do not
like, it carves out an exception. See generally Marsh v.
Chambers, 463 U.S. 783 (1983). And another. See
generally Lynch v. Donnelly, 465 U.S. 668 (1984). And
another. Van Orden v. Perry, 545 U.S. 677, 685 (2005).
And what you have left “invite[s] chaos in lower courts,
[leads] to differing results in materially identical
cases, and create[s] a minefield for legislators.”
Kennedy, 597 U.S. at 534. The Court has started down
this path in the Free Exercise Clause context, except
the situation is far more dire. Instead of carving out
exceptions from a single test  from a single case, this
Court is carving exceptions out of everything.
When Congress passed the Religious Land Use and
Institutionalized Persons Act in 2000, it was aware of
Williamson County’s requirement of a final decision in
land-use cases. The judiciary had been imposing that

15
requirement on land-use cases regularly for 15 years.
City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes , 526 U.S. 687
(1999); Suitum v. Tahoe Reg’l Planning Agency , 520
U.S. 725, 737 (1997); Macdonald v. County of Yolo, 477
U.S. 340, 349 (1986). Thus, when Congress declared
that “[n]o government shall impose or implement a
land use regulation in a manner that imposes a
substantial burden on the religious exercise of a
person, including a religious assembly or institution”
unless it can survive strict scrutiny, 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc(a)(1) (emphasis added), it was well aware
that this Court does not consider a land use regulation
to be imposed “until a final decision is made as to how
the regulations will be applied to respondent's property.”
Williamson County, 473 U.S. at 200. A holding from
this Court that anyone seeking to use their land a
particular way for religious reasons need not wait for
a final decision from the regulating body would both
directly conflict with RLUIPA, which does not provide
a cause of action until the land use regulation has been
“imposed,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc(a)(1), and invites all the
issues that the Williamson County  finality requirement is meant to avoid.
Moreover, it would set a pre cedent that is deeply
disturbing in its implications: Article III’s universal,
well-understood, concrete injury requirement suddenly
would not apply  to religious claims. If a litigant’s
motivations are religious, they need not wait for the
government to actually do  anything. The established
rules do not apply. Such a decision could have immediate consequences far beyond the land-use context.
1. Prisons
Just as Williamson County  established one of the
criteria of ripeness for land-use claims in general, the
Prison Litigation Reform Act imposes distinct ripeness

16
requirements on causes of action brought by institutionalized persons in general, including the requirement
that the prospective litigant exhaust their existing
administrative remedies before seeking redress in
court. 42 U.S.C. § 1997e. However, a decision from this
Court declaring even a procedural delay to be too high
a burden on religious exercise in land-use cases could
readily be applied to religious claims brought by
prisoners. Just as a decision in favor of Mr. Grand in
this case would create a two-tiered classification of
land owners (i.e., on the one hand, those putting their
land to religious uses who face far fewer barriers to
litigation and, on the other hand, those who are
putting their land to whatev er legal use they see fit
and therefore must clear all regulatory hurdles before
being granted access to the courts) that incentivizes
religious land use over any other use, so too would a
two-tiered classification of institutionalized persons be
created, further incentivizing religiosity in a setting
where individuals already feel immense pressure to
conform to religious demands. See generally Miller v.
Marshall, 682 F. Supp. 3d 559 (S.D. W. Va. 2023).
2. Tax lawsuits
Challenges to the collection  of federal income taxes
predate the Sixteenth Amendment. See generally
Pollock v. Farmers’ Loan & Trust Co. , 157 U.S. 429
(1895). Those challenging the federal income tax or
some aspect of it frequently point to religious beliefs
as the justification. See generally Hernandez v.
Comm’r, 490 U.S. 680 (1989); United States v. Lee, 455
U.S. 252 (1982); United States v. Am. Friends Serv.
Comm, 419 U.S. 7 (1974). Those who seek to challenge
the government’s collection of tax revenue frequently
run up against the “pay-now-sue-later” procedures
imposed by the Anti-Injunction Act, 26 U.S.C.

17
§ 7421(a), which requires those wishing to challenge a
tax levied upon them to first pay the tax and then sue
for a refund. CIC Servs., LLC v. IRS, 593 U.S. 209, 222
(2021).
Similarly, the Tax Injunction Act requires would-be
litigants seeking to challen ge “the assessment, levy
or collection of any tax under State law” to take
advantage of state regimes for challenging taxes. 28
U.S.C. § 1341. The federal judiciary only has jurisdiction where state law fails to provide “a plain, speedy
and efficient remedy” for a tax dispute. Id.
However, should this Court holds that the delay
resulting from applying for and receiving a special use
permit, variance, or other authorization to use land for
a religious purpose is too great a burden on religious
exercise, it would hardly be a leap for the courts to say
that handing over one’s hard-earned money imposes
an even greater burden and that to require taxpayers
who object to a tax on religious grounds to nonetheless
pay the tax before seeking a remedy in court violates
their free exercise rights. And now we have a twotiered classification system for taxpayers as well, one
in which some who object to a tax get to keep their
funds while pursuing their challenge while the rest
must fork over their mone y and only then may they
ask nicely to please have it back.

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, amicus urges this Court
to AFFIRM the Sixth Circuit’s decision.
